skills.name: benchmarking
skills.description: Guide for building, running, and analyzing Nanvix performance benchmarks. Use this when asked about benchmark setup, execution, or interpretation.

skills.name: build
skills.description: Guide for building, formatting, linting, and spell-checking Nanvix with z. Use this when asked to build or validate the repository.

skills.name: ci-cd-pipeline
skills.description: Guide for Nanvix CI and GitHub Actions workflow behavior, including local pipeline execution and matrix coverage. Use this when asked about CI checks, workflow failures, or release flow.

skills.name: coding-standards
skills.description: Detailed Nanvix coding, documentation, and review standards across Rust, C/C++, Python, and Shell. Use this when asked to implement or review code quality conventions.

skills.name: daemon-development
skills.description: Guide for developing and debugging Nanvix daemons, including guest daemons and host linuxd behavior. Use this when asked about daemon architecture or daemon changes.

skills.name: gdb-debugging
skills.description: Guide for debugging Nanvix guests using GDB remote debugging over the microvm machine type. Use this when asked about attaching GDB, setting breakpoints, or stepping through kernel code.

skills.name: kernel-development
skills.description: Guide for modifying and debugging the Nanvix kernel architecture and kernel-call paths. Use this when asked about kernel internals or kernel implementation changes.

skills.name: library-development
skills.description: Guide for creating and modifying Nanvix libraries under src/libs, including guest no_std and host std crates. Use this when asked about library architecture or crate changes.

skills.name: test
skills.description: Guide for running Nanvix tests with z. Use this when asked to run unit tests, integration tests, or the full test suite.

skills.name: test-development
skills.description: Guide for writing, running, and debugging Nanvix unit, integration, and system tests in Rust and C/C++. Use this when asked about test implementation or failures.

skills.name: troubleshooting
skills.description: Guide for diagnosing Nanvix build, runtime, and test failures, including cleanup and debugging workflows. Use this when asked to investigate errors or unstable behavior.

skills.name: user-app-development
skills.description: Guide for developing, building, and running Nanvix user-space applications across supported runtimes and languages. Use this when asked about guest app implementation or execution.

skills.name: pptx
skills.description: Use this skill any time a .pptx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates, layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.

skills.name: ast-consistency
skills.description: AST-level exec fidelity checking tools and pre-approved deviations. Use after modifying source files to verify exec code is unchanged.

skills.name: body-removal
skills.description: Remove function bodies from Rust/Verus source files to produce signature-only views. Used before the view-design phase to prevent implementation anchoring.

skills.name: bug-reporting
skills.description: Classify and report bugs found during Verus verification. Distinguishes true bugs from missing constraints and verifier limitations. Use when a verification failure might indicate a code bug.

skills.name: caller-analysis
skills.description: Analyze callers of a Rust module to understand usage expectations for Verus verification. Produces a caller-perspective analysis covering all functions with their visibility and call relationships.

skills.name: crate-analysis
skills.description: Principles for verification order in multi-file Rust crates. Verify leaf modules first so downstream modules can reference upstream specs directly. The pipeline tool handles ordering automatically.

skills.name: proof-extraction
skills.description: Extract large inline proof blocks from exec code into named lemmas in .proof.rs. Use when polishing verified code to improve readability and proof organization.

skills.name: proof-minimization
skills.description: Remove redundant proof artifacts (assertions, lemmas, hints, dead code) without weakening guarantees. Use when polishing verified code to reduce verbosity.

skills.name: property-analysis
skills.description: How to analyze source code and identify verification properties — the WHAT of verification. Covers module understanding, property discovery across four dimensions (functional correctness, safety, liveness, structural consistency), and quality review. Use this skill when deciding what to verify for a new module, writing property_analysis.md, or updating global_properties.md.

skills.name: proving-guide
skills.description: Proving methodology and mindset for Verus verification: function-by-function approach, persistence through failures, clean verification, and bug reporting. Use when writing proofs or resolving verification failures.

skills.name: review-methodology
skills.description: Review Verus verification code with focus on spec quality and automated checks.

skills.name: spec-completeness
skills.description: Detect specification incompleteness via nondeterminism checking. Given a Verus function spec, automatically determine whether the spec uniquely determines the output for each valid input. If not, use type-guided binary search to construct a concrete witness (input + two valid but different outputs). No LLM needed — pure SMT-based.

skills.name: spec-design
skills.description: How to write good Verus specs. Covers spec quality principles (anti-patterns, error paths), spec classification (internal, external-top, external-bottom trust boundaries), View abstraction design, and static vs dynamic enforcement. Use when writing or reviewing Verus specs.

skills.name: verus-constraints
skills.description: Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers attribute-based syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code.

skills.name: verus-setup
skills.description: Set up Verus formal verification infrastructure for a Rust project. Covers workspace-level config (vstd dependency, cfg flags, version pinning, Makefile, scripts) and per-crate config (metadata, cfg-gated includes, spec/proof stubs). Use this skill when preparing a repo or crate for Verus verification, adding make verify support, or integrating cheating detection into a build.

skills.name: verus-syntax
skills.description: Verus attribute-based syntax reference for exec functions. Covers #[verus_spec], #[verus_verify], proof!{}, proof_decl!{}, loop invariants. See GUIDE.md for advanced patterns, syntax_attr.rs for the official example.

skills.name: view-design
skills.description: How to design a View type that represents abstract state from the caller's perspective. Input: caller analysis + property concepts. Must NOT see implementation code.

skills.name: customize-cloud-agent
skills.description: Skill for customizing the Copilot cloud agent (formerly known as Copilot coding agent) environment, including copilot-setup-steps.yml configuration, preinstalling tools and dependencies, runners, and settings.

1. // Copyright(c) The Maintainers of Nanvix.
2. // Licensed under the MIT License.
3. 
4. // Cache - Specifications
5. //
6. // This file contains the CacheView type, invariant, spec transition functions,
7. // and View trait implementations for Cache and CacheGuard.
8. 
9. verus! {
10. 
11. //==================================================================================================
12. // External Type Specifications
13. //==================================================================================================
14. 
15. // BTreeMap is from alloc::collections. vstd provides specs in vstd::std_specs::btree,
16. // but they require cfg(std) which is incompatible with this crate's no_std kernel target.
17. // We declare it as an external type so Verus can reference it.
18. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(K)]
19. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(V)]
20. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(A)]
21. #[verifier::external_type_specification]
22. #[verifier::external_body]
23. pub struct ExBTreeMap<K, V, A>(alloc::collections::BTreeMap<K, V, A>)
24.     where A: core::alloc::Allocator + core::clone::Clone;
25. 
26. #[verifier::external_type_specification]
27. pub struct ExGlobal(alloc::alloc::Global);
28. 
29. // CacheEntry is a private internal type.
30. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(V)]
31. #[verifier::external_type_specification]
32. struct ExCacheEntry<V>(crate::CacheEntry<V>);
33. 
34. // CacheGuard wraps &mut V; Verus cannot handle &mut in struct fields,
35. // so we declare it as an external type.
36. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(V)]
37. #[verifier::external_type_specification]
38. #[verifier::external_body]
39. pub struct ExCacheGuard<'a, V>(crate::CacheGuard<'a, V>);
40. 
41. //==================================================================================================
42. // CacheView - Abstract Specification Model
43. //==================================================================================================
44. 
45. /// Abstract view of a bounded LRU cache.
46. ///
47. /// - `contents`: the key-value mapping of all cached entries.
48. /// - `capacity`: maximum number of entries.
49. /// - `lru_order`: keys ordered from LRU (index 0) to MRU (last element).
50. #[verifier::ext_equal]
51. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(K)]
52. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(V)]
53. pub struct CacheView<K, V> {
54.     pub contents: Map<K, V>,
55.     pub capacity: nat,
56.     pub lru_order: Seq<K>,
57. }
58. 
59. impl<K, V> CacheView<K, V> {
60. 
61.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
62.     // Well-formedness Invariant
63.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
64. 
65.     /// Well-formedness invariant for the abstract cache state.
66.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
67.         // Size never exceeds capacity.
68.         &&& self.contents.dom().len() <= self.capacity
69.         // LRU order has no duplicates.
70.         &&& self.lru_order.no_duplicates()
71.         // LRU order contains exactly the stored keys.
72.         &&& self.lru_order.to_set() == self.contents.dom()
73.         // Explicit cardinality link (helps the solver).
74.         &&& self.lru_order.len() == self.contents.dom().len()
75.     }
76. 
77.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
78.     // Helper Spec Functions
79.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
80. 
81.     /// Move `key` to the most-recently-used position (end of the sequence).
82.     /// Preserves all other elements and their relative order.
83.     pub open spec fn move_to_mru(self, key: K) -> Seq<K> {
84.         self.lru_order.filter(|k: K| k != key).push(key)
85.     }
86. 
87.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
88.     // Spec Transition Functions
89.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
90. 
91.     /// Spec transition for `Cache::new`.
92.     pub open spec fn spec_new(capacity: nat) -> CacheView<K, V> {
93.         CacheView {
94.             contents: Map::empty(),
95.             capacity,
96.             lru_order: Seq::empty(),
97.         }
98.     }
99. 
100.     /// Spec transition for `Cache::get`.
101.     /// Returns the updated cache state and the lookup result.
102.     pub open spec fn spec_get(self, key: K) -> (CacheView<K, V>, Option<V>) {
103.         if self.contents.dom().contains(key) {
104.             (CacheView {
105.                 lru_order: self.move_to_mru(key),
106.                 ..self
107.             }, Some(self.contents[key]))
108.         } else {
109.             (self, None)
110.         }
111.     }
112. 
113.     /// Spec transition for `Cache::put`.
114.     pub open spec fn spec_put(self, key: K, value: V) -> CacheView<K, V> {
115.         if self.capacity == 0 {
116.             // Zero-capacity cache: no-op.
117.             self
118.         } else if self.contents.dom().contains(key) {
119.             // Overwrite existing key: replace value, refresh recency.
120.             CacheView {
121.                 contents: self.contents.insert(key, value),
122.                 lru_order: self.move_to_mru(key),
123.                 ..self
124.             }
125.         } else if self.contents.dom().len() >= self.capacity {
126.             // At capacity with new key: evict LRU victim, then insert.
127.             let victim = self.lru_order[0];
128.             CacheView {
129.                 contents: self.contents.remove(victim).insert(key, value),
130.                 lru_order: self.lru_order.subrange(1, self.lru_order.len() as int).push(key),
131.                 ..self
132.             }
133.         } else {
134.             // Below capacity with new key: insert directly.
135.             CacheView {
136.                 contents: self.contents.insert(key, value),
137.                 lru_order: self.lru_order.push(key),
138.                 ..self
139.             }
140.         }
141.     }
142. 
143.     /// Spec transition for `Cache::remove`.
144.     pub open spec fn spec_remove(self, key: K) -> CacheView<K, V> {
145.         if self.contents.dom().contains(key) {
146.             CacheView {
147.                 contents: self.contents.remove(key),
148.                 lru_order: self.lru_order.filter(|k: K| k != key),
149.                 ..self
150.             }
151.         } else {
152.             // Key absent: no-op.
153.             self
154.         }
155.     }
156. 
157.     /// Spec transition for `Cache::clear`.
158.     pub open spec fn spec_clear(self) -> CacheView<K, V> {
159.         CacheView {
160.             contents: Map::empty(),
161.             lru_order: Seq::empty(),
162.             ..self  // capacity preserved
163.         }
164.     }
165. }
166. 
167. //==================================================================================================
168. // View Implementation for Cache
169. //==================================================================================================
170. 
171. // vstd BTreeMap specs require cfg(std), unavailable on this no_std target.
172. // The view is therefore uninterpreted; constraints come from external_body ensures clauses.
173. impl<K: Ord + Clone, V> View for Cache<K, V> {
174.     type V = CacheView<K, V>;
175. 
176.     uninterp spec fn view(&self) -> CacheView<K, V>;
177. }
178. 
179. //==================================================================================================
180. // View Implementation for CacheGuard
181. //==================================================================================================
182. 
183. // CacheGuard is external_body (Verus limitation: &mut in struct fields),
184. // so the view is uninterpreted. Constraints come from get/deref ensures.
185. impl<'a, V> View for CacheGuard<'a, V> {
186.     type V = V;
187. 
188.     uninterp spec fn view(&self) -> V;
189. }
190. 
191. } // verus!

name: verus-constraints
description: "Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers attribute-based syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code."
---

# Verus Constraints

Study `docs/examples/binary-search/proof/` for a complete example following all
constraints below.

## Attribute Style for Exec Functions

All specs on **exec functions** must use the attribute-based syntax
(`#[verus_spec]`, `#[verus_verify]`, `proof! { }`, `proof_decl! { }`).
See the **verus-syntax** skill for the full reference and examples.

```rust
// ✅ CORRECT — attribute style for exec functions
#[verus_spec(ret =>
    requires x < 100,
    ensures ret == x + 1,
)]
fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 {
    x + 1
}

// ❌ WRONG — do not wrap exec functions in verus! { }
verus! {
    fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
        requires x < 100,
        ensures ret == x + 1,
    { x + 1 }
} // verus!
```

**`verus! { }` blocks** are still used for:
- `spec fn` and `proof fn` definitions (in `.spec.rs` and `.proof.rs`)
- Type-level specs (`broadcast`, `impl View`, etc.)

Key benefit: exec function signatures stay unmodified — the original `fn`
signature is untouched, specs live in the attribute.

## Source Integrity (exec code)

The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
`*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.

Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Keep changes
minimal so developers can review diffs easily.

**Preserve by default:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions,
comments, debug assertions, and all other existing code.

**Minimal equivalent rewrites** are allowed when Verus genuinely cannot express
a construct. The escalation ladder (each step requires exhausting the previous):

1. **Verify as-is** — most code works with Verus directly.
2. **Search vstd** — your training data is likely outdated. `grep -r` the entire
   vstd directory. Check `std_specs/`, recent additions.
3. **Minimal equivalent rewrite** — rewrite the smallest possible expression
   to an equivalent one Verus accepts. Requirements:
   - Same semantics (identical observable behavior for all inputs)
   - Same panic/error behavior
   - Same asymptotic time and space complexity
   - Smallest possible diff
   - `// VERUS REWRITE: <reason>` comment on the changed code
   - Minimal reproducer proving the original is unsupported
4. **Stdlib wrapper** — if a stdlib/core function call fails because Verus
   cannot handle the parameter types (e.g., `&mut [T]` from `DerefMut`
   coercion, closures), create a thin wrapper function whose body contains
   **ONLY** the stdlib call. Mark the wrapper `external_body` with pre/post
   conditions. The original function calls the wrapper instead. This isolates
   the trust boundary to the thinnest possible layer.

   Example — `core::mem::replace` on `&mut Vec<T>[index]`:
   ```rust
   #[verus_verify(external_body)]
   #[verus_spec(prev =>
       requires index < old(v)@.len(),
       ensures
           prev == old(v)@[index as int],
           v@ == old(v)@.update(index as int, value),
           v@.len() == old(v)@.len(),
   )]
   fn vec_replace<T>(v: &mut Vec<T>, index: usize, value: T) -> T {
       ::core::mem::replace(&mut v[index], value)
   }
   ```
   The wrapper body is a single stdlib call. The `external_body` trusts only
   this one line. The calling function remains fully body-verified.

5. **`external_body` on the original** — absolute last resort. Requires a
   minimal reproducer and `trust.md` entry.

**Principle:** prefer rewriting code to a semantic equivalent over ANY cheating.
A rewrite that lets Verus verify the body is always better than `external_body`.

**Never cfg-gate away and duplicate exec definitions.** Adding
`#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` to a function, impl block, struct, enum, or
constant and providing a verus-annotated copy is forbidden — it verifies the
copy, not the real code, and the two will silently diverge.

- **Functions / impl blocks**: add contracts to the original in-place.

2. Need to also add `View` impl for `BTreeMap` since the vstd one is gated behind `cfg(std)`
3. Remove `external_body` from `Cache::new`
4. Run `make verify-cache`

The reviewer noted that vstd does NOT have BTreeMap specs in this version (my search confirmed it - there's no btree.rs in vstd/std_specs/). But the reviewer mentions it exists in some version. Since there's no btree.rs, I need to write the `assume_specification` myself.


Looking at the current `lib.spec.rs`, I see `ExBTreeMap` is already defined as an external type specification with an external body, and the `Cache` view is uninterpreted. The real problem is that `BTreeMap::new()` lacks a specification, and I need to connect the BTreeMap view to the Cache view so the verification understands what's happening.

I need to add an `assume_specification` for `BTreeMap::new` that describes it returning an empty BTreeMap, and provide a `View` implementation for `BTreeMap<K, V>` itself. The reviewer's feedback is clear—I should add a local `assume_specification` for `alloc::collections::BTreeMap::new` following the vstd pattern, and remove the `external_body` from `Cache` to make it interpretable. The issue is that the `Cache` view is currently uninterpreted, so if I remove `external_body` from `Cache::new`, Verus won't be able to verify the ensures clause since it can't reason about what `result@` actually is. I need to either keep the `external_body` annotation or provide a concrete view implementation that connects the view to the actual struct fields. Verus won't know anything about it. The ensures say `result@ == spec_new(capacity as nat)` which expands to:
```
CacheView {
    contents: Map::empty(),
    capacity: capacity as nat,
    lru_order: Seq::empty(),
}
```

Since the view is uninterpreted, Verus can't connect `Cache { entries: BTreeMap::new(), counter: 0, capacity }` to `CacheView { contents: Map::empty(), ... }`.

The core issue is that I have an `assume_specification` for `BTreeMap::new` with `ensures m@ == Map::<K, V>::empty()`, but the `View` for `BTreeMap` itself is uninterpreted. Inside `Cache::new`, Verus needs to prove `result@ == CacheView::spec_new(capacity as nat)`, but since `Cache`'s view is also uninterpreted, it doesn't know how to relate the fields to the view. The solution is to make `Cache`'s view interpreted instead, mapping the BTreeMap's view to the CacheView structure.

However, this is extremely complex because `contents` needs to extract just the values from `BTreeMap<K, CacheEntry<V>>` into a `Map<K, V>`, and `lru_order` needs to be derived by sorting entries by their counter field. That's probably why the view was left uninterpreted in the first place.

The reviewer acknowledges this complexity and suggests that if new errors appear around the uninterpreted `view()`, we should report them and address it next turn. So my plan is to add an uninterpreted `View` for `BTreeMap<K, V, A>` following vstd's pattern, add an `assume_specification` for `BTreeMap::new()` that ensures the map is empty, remove `external_body` from `Cache::new`, and then run verification to see what happens. I need to be careful about the `const fn` constraint since both `Cache::new` and `BTreeMap::new()` are const functions.

4. // Cache - Specifications
5. //
6. // This file contains the CacheView type, invariant, spec transition functions,
7. // and View trait implementations for Cache and CacheGuard.
8. 
9. verus! {
10. 
11. //==================================================================================================
12. // External Type Specifications
13. //==================================================================================================
14. 
15. // BTreeMap is from alloc::collections. vstd provides specs in vstd::std_specs::btree,
16. // but they require cfg(std) which is incompatible with this crate's no_std kernel target.
17. // We declare it as an external type so Verus can reference it.
18. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(K)]
19. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(V)]
20. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(A)]
21. #[verifier::external_type_specification]
22. #[verifier::external_body]
23. pub struct ExBTreeMap<K, V, A>(alloc::collections::BTreeMap<K, V, A>)
24.     where A: core::alloc::Allocator + core::clone::Clone;
25. 
26. #[verifier::external_type_specification]
27. pub struct ExGlobal(alloc::alloc::Global);
28. 
29. //==================================================================================================
30. // BTreeMap View & assume_specification (mirroring vstd::std_specs::btree, gated behind cfg(std))
31. //==================================================================================================
32. 
33. // View for BTreeMap via proxy type — works around orphan rules since ExBTreeMap is local.
34. // Matches vstd pattern at vstd/std_specs/btree.rs:457-461.
35. impl<Key, Value, A: core::alloc::Allocator + core::clone::Clone> View for ExBTreeMap<Key, Value, A> {
36.     type V = Map<Key, Value>;
37.     uninterp spec fn view(&self) -> Map<Key, Value>;
38. }
39. 
40. // assume_specification for BTreeMap::new — matches vstd/std_specs/btree.rs:613-616.
41. // Uses ExBTreeMap (external_type_specification proxy) in return position so m@ resolves.
42. pub assume_specification<K, V>[ alloc::collections::BTreeMap::<K, V>::new ]()
43.     -> (m: ExBTreeMap<K, V, alloc::alloc::Global>)
44.     ensures
45.         m@ == Map::<K, V>::empty(),
46. ;
47. 
48. // CacheEntry is a private internal type.
49. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(V)]
50. #[verifier::external_type_specification]
51. struct ExCacheEntry<V>(crate::CacheEntry<V>);
52. 
53. // CacheGuard wraps &mut V; Verus cannot handle &mut in struct fields,
54. // so we declare it as an external type.
55. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(V)]
56. #[verifier::external_type_specification]
57. #[verifier::external_body]
58. pub struct ExCacheGuard<'a, V>(crate::CacheGuard<'a, V>);
59. 
60. //==================================================================================================
61. // CacheView - Abstract Specification Model
62. //==================================================================================================
63. 
64. /// Abstract view of a bounded LRU cache.
65. ///
66. /// - `contents`: the key-value mapping of all cached entries.
67. /// - `capacity`: maximum number of entries.
68. /// - `lru_order`: keys ordered from LRU (index 0) to MRU (last element).
69. #[verifier::ext_equal]
70. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(K)]
71. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(V)]
72. pub struct CacheView<K, V> {
73.     pub contents: Map<K, V>,
74.     pub capacity: nat,
75.     pub lru_order: Seq<K>,
76. }
77. 
78. impl<K, V> CacheView<K, V> {
79. 
80.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
81.     // Well-formedness Invariant
82.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
83. 
84.     /// Well-formedness invariant for the abstract cache state.
85.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
86.         // Size never exceeds capacity.
87.         &&& self.contents.dom().len() <= self.capacity
88.         // LRU order has no duplicates.
89.         &&& self.lru_order.no_duplicates()
90.         // LRU order contains exactly the stored keys.
91.         &&& self.lru_order.to_set() == self.contents.dom()
92.         // Explicit cardinality link (helps the solver).
93.         &&& self.lru_order.len() == self.contents.dom().len()
94.     }
95. 
96.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
97.     // Helper Spec Functions
98.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
99. 
100.     /// Move `key` to the most-recently-used position (end of the sequence).
101.     /// Preserves all other elements and their relative order.
102.     pub open spec fn move_to_mru(self, key: K) -> Seq<K> {
103.         self.lru_order.filter(|k: K| k != key).push(key)
104.     }
105. 
106.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
107.     // Spec Transition Functions
108.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
109. 
110.     /// Spec transition for `Cache::new`.
111.     pub open spec fn spec_new(capacity: nat) -> CacheView<K, V> {
112.         CacheView {
113.             contents: Map::empty(),
114.             capacity,
115.             lru_order: Seq::empty(),
116.         }
117.     }
118. 
119.     /// Spec transition for `Cache::get`.
120.     /// Returns the updated cache state and the lookup result.
121.     pub open spec fn spec_get(self, key: K) -> (CacheView<K, V>, Option<V>) {
122.         if self.contents.dom().contains(key) {
123.             (CacheView {
124.                 lru_order: self.move_to_mru(key),
125.                 ..self
126.             }, Some(self.contents[key]))
127.         } else {
128.             (self, None)
129.         }
130.     }
131. 
132.     /// Spec transition for `Cache::put`.
133.     pub open spec fn spec_put(self, key: K, value: V) -> CacheView<K, V> {
134.         if self.capacity == 0 {
135.             // Zero-capacity cache: no-op.
136.             self
137.         } else if self.contents.dom().contains(key) {
138.             // Overwrite existing key: replace value, refresh recency.
139.             CacheView {
140.                 contents: self.contents.insert(key, value),
141.                 lru_order: self.move_to_mru(key),
142.                 ..self
143.             }
144.         } else if self.contents.dom().len() >= self.capacity {
145.             // At capacity with new key: evict LRU victim, then insert.
146.             let victim = self.lru_order[0];
147.             CacheView {
148.                 contents: self.contents.remove(victim).insert(key, value),
149.                 lru_order: self.lru_order.subrange(1, self.lru_order.len() as int).push(key),
150.                 ..self
151.             }
152.         } else {
153.             // Below capacity with new key: insert directly.
154.             CacheView {
155.                 contents: self.contents.insert(key, value),
156.                 lru_order: self.lru_order.push(key),
157.                 ..self
158.             }
159.         }
160.     }
161. 
162.     /// Spec transition for `Cache::remove`.
163.     pub open spec fn spec_remove(self, key: K) -> CacheView<K, V> {
164.         if self.contents.dom().contains(key) {
165.             CacheView {
166.                 contents: self.contents.remove(key),
167.                 lru_order: self.lru_order.filter(|k: K| k != key),
168.                 ..self
169.             }
170.         } else {
171.             // Key absent: no-op.
172.             self
173.         }
174.     }
175. 
176.     /// Spec transition for `Cache::clear`.
177.     pub open spec fn spec_clear(self) -> CacheView<K, V> {
178.         CacheView {
179.             contents: Map::empty(),
180.             lru_order: Seq::empty(),
181.             ..self  // capacity preserved
182.         }
183.     }
184. }
185. 
186. //==================================================================================================
187. // View Implementation for Cache
188. //==================================================================================================
189. 
190. // vstd BTreeMap specs require cfg(std), unavailable on this no_std target.
191. // The view is therefore uninterpreted; constraints come from external_body ensures clauses.
192. impl<K: Ord + Clone, V> View for Cache<K, V> {
193.     type V = CacheView<K, V>;
194. 
195.     uninterp spec fn view(&self) -> CacheView<K, V>;
196. }
197. 
198. //==================================================================================================
199. // View Implementation for CacheGuard
200. //==================================================================================================
201. 
202. // CacheGuard is external_body (Verus limitation: &mut in struct fields),
203. // so the view is uninterpreted. Constraints come from get/deref ensures.
204. impl<'a, V> View for CacheGuard<'a, V> {
205.     type V = V;
206. 
207.     uninterp spec fn view(&self) -> V;
208. }
209. 
210. } // verus!
